text.p: Malaysia's city of the future begins to emerge from a swathe of jungle and plantations on Saturday with the launch of Cyberjaya, a hi-tech city that has attracted some of the world's leading multimedia firms.

Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad will preside at the ground-breaking for Cyberjaya ("cyber-success" in Malay), where every home will have Internet access and all business transactions will be payed for with smart cards.
Aimed at luring top hi-tech firms, the 7,000-hectare (17,300-acre) city is located in the Multimedia Super Corridor (MSC).

A brainchild of Mahathir's, the MSC is a zone 15 km by 50 km (nine miles by 30 miles) -- or about the size of Singapore -- stretching south from Kuala Lumpur to where a new international airport and a new federal capital called Putrajaya are also under construction.

Forty-two foreign and local companies have made firm commitments to locate operations in Cyberjaya. They include U.S. companies AT&T Corp, Sun Microsystems Inc and NCR Corp, Germany's Siemens AG, British Telecommunications Plc and Japan's Mitsubishi Corp, Sumitomo and Sharp.
"Cyberjaya will be a utopia for multimedia development," said Othman Yeop Abdullah, executive chairman of Multimedia Development Corp, which oversees the development of the MSC.
"It will provide the most ideal working and living environment to attract big multimedia players to invest in the MSC," he said.

Developing the city will be Cyberview Sdn Bhd, a joint venture between five Malaysian parties and Japan's Nippon Telegraph and Telephone Corp The initial investment is estimated at 3.5 billion ringgit ($1.4 billion).
The first phase is a 2,800-hectare (6,900-acre) flagship zone expected to be completed by next April. It includes the Malaysian Multimedia University.

First conceived in 1994, the MSC hopes to attract a variety of firms on the "information superhighway" -- from software designers and electronic publishers to film production houses and Internet service providers.
Some of the flagship applications include smart schools that incoporate the Internet and other computer applications.
The corridor is aimed at moving Malaysia up from a low-tech assembler of electronic products for multinational corporations to the cutting edge of the information age.
Its electronic backbone will be a 2.5-10 gigabyte digital fibre-optic network that will link the corridor to Japan, Europe and the United States.
The MSC will initially be driven by three mega-projects that will be major consumers of multimedia products and services.
One is the new capital of Putrajaya, designed to the world's first paperless government hub.
The others are the new airport and the Kuala Lumpur City Centre, a massive office project featuring the Petronas Twin Towers, the world's tallest buildings at 452 metres (1,482 feet).
